price_per_million.source: copied from reasoning_models_v1 (confirmed 2026-11-11); thinking tokens billed as output

research_concepts: opponent next-possession PPP (T+1) after play type X
methodological_questions: Is the play-type-specific opponent T+1 PPP shift large enough, relative to direct PPP differences, to change an AVOID label?
Do own-sequence lags show decaying, play-type-specific memory once within-team baselines are used?
Can the shift be separated from the mechanical effect of how the preceding possession ended (made basket, miss, turnover, foul)?
Are the inferred play-type labels reliable enough to attribute T+1 effects to a specific play type?
How should multiplicity and small cells be handled across play type x lag x team or player?

historical_evidence.finding: Extended Possession Value: 4 of 8 play types showed a 'real' opponent T+1 suppression (CUT +0.0220, TRANSITION +0.0145, SPOT_UP +0.0124, POST_UP +0.0194). DRIVE was not real (+0.0024). The record states the downstream effects are small (~0.01-0.02 PPP) relative to direct PPP gaps, and that player-level results were mostly non-findings after BH correction.

Persistent Impact Score Level 1 gate FAILED the decay sanity check. DRIVE lifts were flat across lags (+0.015 to +0.021). Within-team, lag-1 fell to between +0.015 and -0.002. Cohen d was ~0.01-0.03 with p~0 from n>150k. Callable play-type horizons = 0. The record attributes this to team-quality confounding (n=915,570 possessions).

Defensive aftershock after success was found for 8/8 play types, all-games and playoffs, at roughly +0.12 to +0.135 PPP (e.g. CUT +0.119, n=21,398). Pair premiums were also reported (e.g. PUTBACK->TRANSITION +0.084, n=565). The record is limited by small samples in some cells; the full text is truncated in the retrieval result.

Star-level sequential suppression: PUTBACK was the top suppressor for 6+ stars (e.g. Mitchell d=-0.294, n_after=95). The record notes no multiplicity correction, n_after of 30-95 for several cells, and a drift/nonstationarity risk.

Play-type label audit FAILED overall: OTHER is 20.2% against a <10% target, 40.8% of labels are low confidence, DRIVE foul-draw rate is 1.7% against a 14-22% benchmark, and foul possessions leak into OTHER. The record says label issues 'undermine adaptation findings'.
OTHER PPP is inflated by 36% foul endings, DRIVE is 12pp below the foul benchmark, and initiation_type maps only 0.7% of 50,668 possessions to a real play type.

The assisted flag exists only on makes, which produced SPOT_UP 2.83 PPP (100% makes) and TRANSITION 0.62 PPP. After the classifier rewrite, values were ~1.16 and ~1.20. The record says this poisoned earlier simulation work.

Within-game and cross-game defensive scheme change could not be separated from label noise (near-uniform transition matrices; inferred labels cannot separate defensive adjustment from offensive execution).
Observed on-ball defensive scheme labels were available for only 14.9% (DET) and 3.3% (ORL) of possessions; switches_on was unpopulated.

Holdout games with a play-type mix closer to the model's recommended mix scored better (strength-controlled +3.27 ORtg, n=908 rows, same-pipeline validation only). It does not address T+1 effects directly.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using flat lag-1..lag-5 pooled lifts as evidence of play-type cross-possession memory
failed_approaches.why: Lifts did not decay and collapsed under a within-team baseline; the record gives a team-quality confound and notes that tiny effects (d~0.01-0.03) are 'significant' only because n>150k.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Possession-level PPP by inferred play type from a classifier using an assisted flag
failed_approaches.why: The flag exists only on makes, so labels were derived from the outcome (C_artifact).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating per-play-type PPP differences as real efficiency
failed_approaches.why: Foul-ending leakage into OTHER and DRIVE, and almost no mapping to initiation_type.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Inferred play-type labels as the basis for adaptation findings
failed_approaches.why: The audit failed (OTHER 20.2%, 40.8% low confidence, benchmark mismatches).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Star-by-star sequential suppression cells with no multiplicity correction
failed_approaches.why: Small n_after (30-95) against large baselines, with a nonstationarity risk.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Inferring defensive scheme change from labels
failed_approaches.why: Label noise cannot be separated from real adjustment.

evidence_establishes: Per FAM:SF-APPS-075 (not a hypothesis test), the recorded play-type-specific opponent T+1 effects are on the order of 0.01-0.02 PPP and are described there as small relative to direct PPP gaps.
Per FAM:SF-CHT-029 (artifact), flat own-sequence lags in the pooled data are not distinguishable from team-quality confounding; decaying, play-type-specific lag memory was not found.

Per FAM:SF07 (supported), an opponent aftershock of ~+0.12 to +0.135 PPP appears for all 8 play types. Its near-uniformity across play types is recorded, but the record does not say it is play-type specific.
Per FAM:SF-APPM-014, FAM:SF-CHT-025 and FAM:SF-PAP-096, earlier play-type labels had documented leakage and label errors that threaten any label-based finding.
evidence_does_not_establish: That any play type's T+1 effect is large enough to change an AVOID label; no record defines an AVOID threshold or tests label flips.
Whether the SF07 aftershock is play-type specific or is a generic effect of how the prior possession ended; the retrieved text is truncated.
Whether any effect survives the rewritten classifier, because several records predate or overlap the classifier rewrite and the post-rewrite label audit status is not shown.
Whether any T+1 effect holds out of sample on 2025-26 data.
own_inferences: The similar ~+0.12 to +0.13 aftershock across all 8 play types in SF07 suggests a generic sequencing mechanism (e.g. the opponent's possession after a make versus a miss, transition-eligible starts), not a play-type-specific causal effect. That would make it unsuitable for AVOID labels.

If the true play-type-specific T+1 effects are ~0.01-0.02 PPP, they are an order of magnitude smaller than typical direct PPP gaps between play types, so AVOID flips would likely be rare or confined to near-threshold play types.
Large-n significance (p~0) will be uninformative here; only effect size relative to a pre-specified label threshold and within-team contrasts matter.
The premise 'large enough to drive AVOID labels' will more likely be rejected or reduced to a few borderline cases than supported.
uncertainties: The AVOID label definition and threshold are not stated in the task, nor in retrieved records.
SF07's full text, the definition of 'after success', and its controls were not read.
The current label quality after the classifier rewrite is unknown.
It is unknown whether the direction of T+1 effects (suppression versus lift) is consistent across records.
2025-26 playoffs are only partial as of 2026-06-19 and complete on 2026-06-21, so any playoff data is incomplete and may change.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history I would have treated this as a straightforward lag regression. The records move the decision to proceed with changes: effects are small (APPS-075), pooled lags are confounded by team quality (CHT-029), the label pipeline has recorded leakage and error (PAP-096, CHT-025, APPM-014), and the star-level cells are underpowered and uncorrected (APPA-050). They also require a pre-specified AVOID threshold, within-team baselines, control for the preceding possession's result, a post-rewrite label audit gate, and an out-of-sample holdout.

blocking_constraints.text: Play-type labels have recorded leakage and misclassification; if the current classifier fails the audit gate, the T+1 attribution cannot be tested.

Team quality, lineup, score state, and the preceding possession's outcome type must be separated from the play-type effect; the pooled lag results in FAM:SF-CHT-029 collapsed under within-team baselines.
Labels that depend on makes (such as the assisted flag) can mechanically shift the next possession (make vs miss), so T+1 effects could be built into the labeling.

prior_work.summary: Earlier records measured opponent T+1 effects and lags. They found small play-type-specific effects (~0.01-0.02 PPP, FAM:SF-APPS-075, not a hypothesis test), flat lags that failed a decay gate under within-team baselines (FAM:SF-CHT-029, artifact), and a uniform aftershock across play types (FAM:SF07, supported). The specific claim that these effects are large enough to drive AVOID labels was not tested, and label quality has repeatedly been an issue.

risks.text: Inferred play-type labels are noisy (OTHER 20%, low confidence 41%, foul leakage), so T+1 attribution to a play type may be biased.
A classifier feature that exists only on makes biased PPP in a prior record; any remaining outcome-dependent features would make T+1 mechanical.
Team quality, opponent quality, lineup, score margin, clock, and the make/miss/turnover context of possession T all confound T+1 PPP.

After a made basket the next possession starts against a set defense; after a miss or turnover it can start in transition. T+1 PPP differs mechanically by how X ended, and play types differ in make rates.
Play type x lag x team or player creates many cells; earlier star-level cells had no correction.
Aggregate n is large, but team-level or star-level cells are small (n_after 30-95); with n>150k, trivial effects give p~0, so size matters more than significance.
AVOID labels chosen from extreme observed T+1 values will regress toward the mean, especially in small cells.
Without placebo checks (shuffled or lead possessions, pre-possession T-1 outcomes), a nonzero lag cannot be told apart from structural dependence in possession sequences.
Pace, spacing, and rules differ across 2022-23 to 2025-26, and playoff versus regular-season behavior differs.
Label inference using later events (made-shot flags, assists, fouls) on the same or following possession leaks outcome into the label.

design.estimand: For each play type X, the within-team, within-opponent difference in opponent T+1 PPP after the team runs X versus its own average after other play types, holding fixed the ending of possession T (make / miss+defensive rebound / turnover / foul), score margin bin, period, and lineup strength. Compared against a pre-registered AVOID threshold: AVOID is flipped only if the T+1-adjusted value (direct PPP minus the T+1 effect) crosses the threshold, and the effect is 'large enough' only if flips occur for at least 1 play type on holdout.
design.unit: Possession pair (T, T+1) within a game, with team-clustered standard errors; the secondary unit is the lag-k sequence for k=1..3 of the team's own possessions.
design.sample: Discovery: 2022-23 to 2024-25 regular seasons (playoffs separate). Holdout: 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13). 2025-26 playoffs are partial before 2026-06-21 and excluded. Exclude end-of-period possessions, garbage time (margin>20 in the last 6 min), and possessions with low-confidence labels (a confident-only main analysis, with a sensitivity analysis including them). Entry gate: the rewritten classifier must pass the label audit (OTHER <10%, DRIVE foul-draw within benchmark, no assist-flag dependence) before any T+1 analysis.
design.power: Pooled by play type, n is tens of thousands per play type; a minimum detectable effect is set below 0.01 PPP, and cluster-robust CIs rather than p-values are used. Team-level and player-level cells are analysed only if n>=300 (otherwise reported as not testable), with empirical-Bayes shrinkage to address RTM. The main outcome is the CI of the effect relative to the pre-specified AVOID threshold, which is fixed before looking at the holdout.
design.controls: Team and opponent fixed effects (within-team baseline), possession-T ending type, score margin, period, clock bucket, lineup net rating, home/away, season. Lag models include lags 1-3 jointly with a decay check (lag-1 >= lag-2 >= lag-3) as in the earlier gate.
design.falsification: (1) Placebo: shuffle play-type labels across possessions within team-game; the effect should vanish. (2) Lead placebo: T-1 play type should not predict T+1 opponent PPP after controlling for T. (3) Label-independent check: replace inferred play types with raw PBP action types (shot distance, assist, turnover) to see whether the effect is label dependent. (4) Uniformity test: if the effect is similar across all 8 play types (as in FAM:SF07), conclude it is generic sequencing and not play-type specific. (5) Gate failure: if the flat-lag/decay check fails after within-team controls (as in FAM:SF-CHT-029), report null.
design.multiplicity: 8 play types x 3 lags = 24 primary tests, Benjamini-Hochberg at q=0.05 within the family; team-level and player-level analyses are exploratory and labeled as such.
design.decision_rule: Support the claim only if, on the 2025-26 holdout, at least one play type has a T+1-adjusted effect whose 95% CI excludes zero, is play-type specific (differs from the all-play-type mean after BH), shows decaying lags, survives the placebos, and flips the AVOID label under the pre-registered threshold. If CIs lie within +/-0.02 PPP and no label flips, report rejection (adequately powered null). If the label audit gate fails, report untestable.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files for 2022-23 to 2024-25 (regular season and playoffs) for discovery; 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13) as the frozen holdout; derived play-type possession records from the graph database, rebuilt with the post-rewrite classifier; data snapshot and classifier commit hash recorded at pre-registration (2026-06-19). 2025-26 playoffs excluded until complete (2026-06-21), then usable only as a secondary replication.

methodological_questions: Is the effect of a play type on the opponent's next-possession points per possession large enough to change AVOID labels?
Do lagged own-sequence possession outcomes carry predictive signal beyond play-type quality?
How should confounding by game state, lineup, and team quality be handled in next-possession analyses?
How reliable are derived play-type labels and how does outcome-derived labeling or regression to the mean affect AVOID classification?
args.query: opponent next-possession PPP after play type, AVOID label, lagged own-sequence effects, play-type labeling data quality

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- search_documents(query): rank further study-family documents by text relevance; returns up to 10 families not yet returned.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

{"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["opponent next-possession PPP", "play-type AVOID labels", "own-sequence lag effects", "play-type possession labeling", "sequential possession dependence"], "methodological_questions": ["Is the effect of a play type on the opponent's next-possession points per possession large enough to change AVOID labels?", "Do lagged own-sequence possession outcomes carry predictive signal beyond play-type quality?", "How should confounding by game state, lineup, and team quality be handled in next-possession analyses?", "How reliable are derived play-type labels and how does outcome-derived labeling or regression to the mean affect AVOID classification?"], "query": "opponent next-possession PPP after play type, AVOID label, lagged own-sequence effects, play-type labeling data quality"}}

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether to pull a couple more family records, since some of the entries are cut off. Budget allows it, but I'm leaning toward finishing with what I have and noting the truncated ones, even though a re-read of one record would give more accuracy.

I'm working out how the historical records bear on whether the effects are large enough to justify AVOID labels. The downstream effects look small, and the supported aftershock effect appears uniform across play types, which points to a mechanical cause rather than anything specific to the plays.

I'm settling the design for the test: relabeling with a rebuilt classifier, comparing against a within-team baseline, controlling for make or miss, and checking the effect size against the AVOID threshold. I'll use 2022-23 through 2024-25 for discovery and the regular season of 2025-26 as the holdout, since the playoffs aren't finished yet. I also have rough probabilities for how the outcome might land, with about 0.6 on the question being testable.

I'm working out how the historical records bear on whether the effects are large enough to justify AVOID labels. The downstream effects look small, and the supported aftershock effect appears uniform across play types, which points to a mechanical cause rather than anything specific to the plays.

I'm settling the design for the test: relabeling with a rebuilt classifier, comparing against a within-team baseline, controlling for make or miss, and checking the effect size against the AVOID threshold. I'll use 2022-23 through 2024-25 for discovery and the regular season of 2025-26 as the holdout, since the playoffs aren't finished yet.
